body:
Primarily, basic tissues are defined based on...

a. Function properties
b. Number of layers
c. Morphology characteristics
d. Shape

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Function properties | **T** | Tissues are grouped by what they do. |
| b. Number of layers | **F** | Layers are used to subclassify epithelia only. |
| c. Morphology characteristics | **T** | Tissues are grouped by their structure. |
| d. Shape | **F** | Cell shape subclassifies epithelia, not the basic tissues. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b F, c T, d F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The four basic tissues (epithelium, connective tissue, muscle, nerve) are defined on their **morphological (structural) and functional characteristics**. Number of layers and cell shape are used only to subclassify epithelium.

## Simplified explanation

Basic tissues are sorted by **what they look like and what they do**.

body:
Epithelial tissues are characterised by...

a. Close cell apposition
b. Extracellular matrix
c. Presence at a free surface
d. Structural support

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Close cell apposition | **T** | Cells are tightly packed with junctions. |
| b. Extracellular matrix | **F** | Epithelium has very little ECM; abundant ECM characterises connective tissue. |
| c. Presence at a free surface | **T** | Epithelia cover surfaces and line cavities. |
| d. Structural support | **F** | Support is a function of connective tissue. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b F, c T, d F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Epithelium is characterised by **close cell apposition** (cells joined by junctional complexes, little intercellular substance) and **presence at a free surface**, resting on a basement membrane. Connective tissue is characterised by abundant extracellular matrix and support functions.

## Simplified explanation

Epithelial cells are **packed tightly** and sit at a **free surface**.

body: Which of the following epithelial tissues lines the interior of blood vessels?

options.hint: Transitional epithelium lines the urinary tract.
Correct. Endothelium is simple squamous epithelium.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Blood vessels and lymphatics are lined by **endothelium**, a **simple squamous epithelium** of flat cells that permits exchange and provides a smooth non-thrombogenic surface.

## Simplified explanation

Blood vessels are lined by thin, flat **simple squamous** cells.

body: A tissue was obtained, processed and stained with haematoxylin and eosin (H&E). From the observation of the stained tissue under the light microscope, the epithelial cells were arranged in a **single layer** and appear **tall and narrow** with the nucleus located to the basal side of the cell. What type of epithelial tissue is that?

options.hint: Transitional is multilayered with dome cells.
Correct. Tall, narrow cells with basal nuclei = (simple) columnar.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Cells **taller than wide** with **basally placed oval nuclei** in a **single layer** form **simple columnar epithelium** (e.g. stomach, intestine, gall bladder).

## Simplified explanation

Tall thin cells in one layer = **columnar** epithelium.

body: Loosely arranged fibres with abundant cells of various types is a characteristic of which tissue type?

options.hint: Dense CT has packed fibres and few cells.
Correct. Areolar (loose) CT has loose fibres and many cell types.
Adipose tissue is mainly fat cells.
Dense irregular CT has packed fibres.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Loose (areolar) connective tissue** has loosely arranged collagen and elastic fibres in abundant ground substance with **many cell types** (fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells, plasma cells, leucocytes). It lies beneath epithelia (lamina propria).

## Simplified explanation

Loose fibres + lots of different cells = **areolar** tissue.

body: Elastic fibres stain with eosin but not well, therefore they cannot always be distinguished from collagen fibres in routine H&E preparation. Which of the following can **selectively** stain elastic fibres?

options.hint: Correct. Weigert's resorcin-fuchsin stains elastic fibres blue-black.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Selective elastic stains: **Weigert's resorcin-fuchsin**, Verhoeff's iron haematoxylin, orcein, aldehyde fuchsin and Miller's. They are often combined with van Gieson counterstain (elastic van Gieson) to show elastic fibres black/blue-black and collagen red.

## Simplified explanation

**Resorcin-fuchsin** stains elastic fibres dark.

body: Typically, the thickness of the basement membrane varies from 15–50 nm. Which of the following stains can be used to demonstrate this structure?

options.hint: Basement membranes are hardly visible with H&E.
Correct. PAS stains the glycoprotein-rich basement membrane magenta.
Not the standard basement membrane stain.

hint: Basement membranes are rich in glycoproteins.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Basement membranes contain type IV collagen, laminin and proteoglycans with abundant carbohydrate, so they are **PAS positive** (magenta). Jones' methenamine silver also blackens them (e.g. glomerular basement membrane).

## Simplified explanation

**PAS** shows the basement membrane.

body:
Which of the following is a **resident** cell type in a connective tissue?

a. Adipose cells
b. Macrophages
c. Fibroblast
d. Neutrophils

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Adipose cells | **T** | Adipocytes are resident cells. |
| b. Macrophages | **T** | Fixed macrophages (histiocytes) are resident. |
| c. Fibroblast | **T** | The main resident cell. |
| d. Neutrophils | **F** | Neutrophils are transient (wandering) cells from blood. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b T, c T, d F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Connective tissue cells are **resident (fixed)** – fibroblasts, myofibroblasts, adipocytes, macrophages (histiocytes), mast cells, mesenchymal stem cells – or **transient (wandering)** – lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils and monocytes, which enter from blood in response to stimuli.

## Simplified explanation

Fibroblasts, fat cells and macrophages live there; **neutrophils** only visit.
hint: Which cells come in from the blood?

body: Reticular fibres may be demonstrated in paraffin sections using...

options.hint: Correct. Reticular fibres are argyrophilic – the classic method (e.g. Gordon and Sweets).
Reticular fibres are weakly PAS-positive, but silver impregnation is the method of choice.
MSB stains fibrin, collagen and red cells.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Reticular (type III collagen) fibres** are **argyrophilic**: silver impregnation methods (Gordon & Sweets, Gomori, Laidlaw) blacken them. Because of their high carbohydrate content they are also PAS-positive, but silver is the standard technique.

## Simplified explanation

Reticular fibres are shown with **silver** stains.

body: In special situations such as interstitial cells of Leydig in the testis and the lutein cells of the ovary, the epithelial cells lack a free surface. The absence of free surface classifies such aggregates as ...

options.hint: Correct. Epithelioid tissue: epithelial-like cells without a free surface.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Aggregates of closely apposed epithelial-like cells that **lack a free surface** – e.g. Leydig cells, lutein cells, islets of Langerhans, adrenal cortex – are called **epithelioid tissue**. They usually derive from mesenchyme and are often endocrine.

## Simplified explanation

Epithelial-looking cells with no free surface = **epithelioid**.

body:
Pseudostratified epithelium can be found at the following site(s)...

a. Trachea
b. Ductus deferens
c. Bronchial tree
d. Colon

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Trachea | **T** | Pseudostratified ciliated columnar (respiratory) epithelium. |
| b. Ductus deferens | **T** | Pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia. |
| c. Bronchial tree | **T** | Bronchi are lined by respiratory (pseudostratified) epithelium. |
| d. Colon | **F** | Simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b T, c T, d F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Pseudostratified columnar epithelium**: all cells touch the basement membrane but nuclei lie at different levels. It lines the **trachea and bronchi** (ciliated, with goblet cells), the **epididymis and ductus deferens** (with stereocilia) and parts of the male urethra. The colon has simple columnar epithelium.

## Simplified explanation

Airways and the sperm duct have pseudostratified lining; the colon does not.

body:
Urothelium is located at the following site(s)...

a. Urethra
b. Bladder
c. Anorectal junction
d. Vagina

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Urethra | **T** | The proximal (prostatic) urethra is lined by urothelium. |
| b. Bladder | **T** | Classic site of transitional epithelium. |
| c. Anorectal junction | **F** | Stratified cuboidal/columnar to stratified squamous. |
| d. Vagina | **F** | Non-keratinised stratified squamous. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b T, c F, d F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Urothelium (transitional epithelium)** lines the urinary passages: renal calyces and pelvis, ureters, **bladder** and the proximal part of the **urethra**. It is a stratified epithelium with large dome-shaped surface (umbrella) cells that flatten when stretched.

## Simplified explanation

Urothelium is found in the **bladder** and the upper **urethra**.

body:
Sweat gland ducts and large ducts of exocrine glands are lined by the following epithelial subtypes.

a. Stratified columnar
b. Stratified cuboidal
c. Simple columnar
d. Simple squamous

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Stratified columnar | **T** | Lines the largest ducts of exocrine glands. |
| b. Stratified cuboidal | **T** | Lines sweat gland ducts and large ducts of exocrine glands. |
| c. Simple columnar | **F** | Lines the gut and smaller ducts. |
| d. Simple squamous | **F** | Lines vessels and serous cavities. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b T, c F, d F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Stratified cuboidal epithelium** (usually two layers) lines **sweat gland ducts** and large exocrine ducts; **stratified columnar** lines the **largest ducts** of exocrine glands, parts of the male urethra and the conjunctiva. Both are uncommon epithelia.

## Simplified explanation

Big gland ducts and sweat ducts have **stratified cuboidal/columnar** linings.

body:
The cell types of connective tissue include...

a. Fibroblasts
b. Mast cells
c. Histiocytes
d. Adipose cells

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Fibroblasts | **T** | The main cell of connective tissue. |
| b. Mast cells | **T** | Resident cells containing heparin/histamine granules. |
| c. Histiocytes | **T** | Tissue macrophages. |
| d. Adipose cells | **T** | Fat-storing cells. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b T, c T, d T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Connective tissue cells include **fibroblasts**, myofibroblasts, **histiocytes (macrophages)**, **mast cells**, **adipocytes**, plasma cells, mesenchymal stem cells and wandering leucocytes.

## Simplified explanation

All four are connective tissue cells.

body: When using the **Masson trichrome** technique, what should be the result for the nuclei?

options.hint: Muscle, cytoplasm and keratin are red.
Correct. Weigert's iron haematoxylin stains nuclei black.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Masson's trichrome** results: **nuclei – black** (Weigert's iron haematoxylin, resistant to the acid dyes), **cytoplasm, muscle, keratin, erythrocytes – red** (acid fuchsin/Biebrich scarlet), **collagen – blue or green** (aniline blue or light green).

## Simplified explanation

Masson's trichrome: nuclei **black**, muscle red, collagen blue.

body: A chemically oxidized staining solution has a shorter shelf-life than a naturally ripened staining solution. This may be due to ...

options.hint: Correct. Chemical oxidants keep oxidising haematein to useless products.
Acid improves selectivity, not shelf life.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Haematoxylin must be oxidised to **haematein**. Chemical oxidants (sodium iodate, mercuric oxide) do this instantly, but oxidation continues and haematein is **over-oxidised** to colourless oxyhaematein, so the solution deteriorates. Naturally (air/light) ripened solutions oxidise slowly and last longer.

## Simplified explanation

Chemical ripening goes too far (**over-oxidation**), so the stain spoils sooner.

body: Thorough washing of sections (in water) before staining is essential because....

options.text: Hydration facilitates the uptake of the dye molecules
options.hint: Correct. Aqueous dyes cannot penetrate a section that still contains wax/solvent or is not hydrated.

hint: Aqueous stains need water in the tissue.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Before aqueous staining, sections are dewaxed (xylene), taken through alcohols and **brought to water**. Proper **hydration** lets aqueous dye solutions penetrate evenly; residual wax or alcohol causes patchy, uneven staining.

## Simplified explanation

Tissues must be **wet (hydrated)** so water-based dyes can get in.

body: Which type of epithelial tissue specializes in moving particles across its surface and is found in the lining of the oviduct and the airways?

options.hint: Correct. Cilia beat to move mucus/ova.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Ciliated** epithelia move material along their surface: **pseudostratified ciliated columnar** epithelium of the airways (mucociliary escalator) and ciliated columnar epithelium of the oviduct (moving the ovum).

## Simplified explanation

Cilia move things along: **pseudostratified ciliated columnar**.

body: What is the name of the tissue that covers the body surfaces, lines body cavities and forms glands?

options.hint: Correct. Covers, lines and forms glands.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Epithelial tissue** covers external surfaces, lines internal cavities and tubes, and forms the secretory parts of **glands** (exocrine and endocrine).

## Simplified explanation

**Epithelium** covers, lines and makes glands.

body: As a Medical Laboratory Scientist at the pathology department, you received a biopsy (human **bladder**) from the surgical ward, preserved in **10% neutral buffered formalin**. Outline the MAJOR stages that you will subject the specimen through before sending it to the pathologist for final microscopic reporting. What morphologic appearance will convince you that the entire process was appropriate and the slide is suitable for routine reporting? *(10 marks)*
answer:
**Major stages**
1. **Reception and accessioning** – check form/label/fixative, assign a lab number.
2. **Adequate fixation** in 10% NBF (6–48 h, ≥10–20× volume).
3. **Grossing** – description, sampling, orientation and placing in labelled cassettes.
4. **Tissue processing** – dehydration (graded alcohols), clearing (xylene), infiltration with molten paraffin wax.
5. **Embedding** – orientate the tissue (urothelial surface perpendicular to the cutting face) in wax blocks.
6. **Microtomy** – trim and cut 3–5 µm sections, float out on a water bath, pick up on clean labelled slides, dry.
7. **Staining** – dewax, hydrate, **H&E** stain, dehydrate, clear.
8. **Mounting** with coverslip (DPX) and labelling; quality control check, then send to the pathologist with the request form.

**Morphology of a good section** – the full thickness is present and correctly oriented; **urothelium** shows several layers of cells with dome-shaped **umbrella cells** at the surface, intact lamina propria and muscularis (detrusor). Nuclei are **crisp blue** with clear chromatin and nuclear membranes; cytoplasm, muscle and collagen show **different shades of pink**; red cells are bright red; no folds, chatter, knife lines, holes, bubbles, pigment or contamination.

> [!answer]
> Reception → fixation → grossing → processing → embedding → microtomy → H&E staining → mounting. Good slide: well-oriented urothelium with umbrella cells, crisp blue nuclei, shades of pink, no artefacts.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Each stage can introduce artefacts: poor fixation (autolysis, smudgy nuclei), poor processing (crumbling, holes), poor microtomy (chatter, folds, thick sections) and poor staining (pale or over-stained nuclei). A good H&E of bladder shows normal **transitional epithelium** with crisp nuclear detail and three shades of eosin.

## Simplified explanation

Receive, fix, cut up, process, block, section, stain with H&E and mount. A good slide shows clear blue nuclei, pink tissue in shades and the bladder's layered lining with no artefacts.
hint: Follow the specimen from reception to coverslip.

body: Many microtomy problems associated with sectioning paraffin, frozen or celloidin tissue blocks are similar. For instance, irregular, skipped or excessively thick and thin sections are usually the result of either too little or too much blade tilt. Mention **six (6)** problems commonly encountered with **paraffin sectioning** in the histopathology laboratory. For each problem suggest **three (3)** ways of preventing it. *(10 marks)*
answer:
| Problem | Prevention / correction |
|---|---|
| **Sections fail to form a ribbon** | Trim top and bottom edges of block parallel; use softer wax or warm the block slightly; reduce knife tilt / use a sharp blade |
| **Thick and thin (alternating/skipped) sections** | Tighten block and knife clamps; correct the clearance angle; check microtome advance mechanism and cool hard blocks |
| **Chatter (venetian-blind lines parallel to the knife)** | Reduce knife tilt/clearance; cut more slowly; soften hard tissue (e.g. surface decalcify or soak the block face in water/softener) |
| **Scores/splits at right angles to the knife** | Change to an undamaged part of the blade; remove hard particles (calcium, sutures, staples); clean wax debris off the knife edge |
| **Compressed, wrinkled sections** | Use a sharp blade; cool the block on ice; reduce the knife angle/cut more slowly |
| **Sections crumble or have holes** | Ensure complete processing (re-process poorly infiltrated tissue); do not over-trim (rough cutting tears tissue); cool block, use sharp knife |
| **Sections curl or stick to block/knife** | Increase clearance angle; clean knife; humidify or use anti-static device |
| **Sections expand/disintegrate on water bath** | Lower bath temperature; re-infiltrate tissue; avoid leaving sections too long on the bath |

> [!answer]
> Any six problems such as poor ribboning, thick/thin sections, chatter, splits, compression, holes/crumbling, curling, disintegration on the bath – each with 3 remedies about the knife, block or processing.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Most microtomy faults are due to the **knife** (blunt, nicked, wrong tilt), the **block** (poor trimming, hardness, temperature, poor processing) or the **microtome** (loose parts). Systematic troubleshooting checks each in turn.

## Simplified explanation

Use a sharp, well-angled blade, a well-trimmed cool block and properly processed tissue to avoid most sectioning problems.

body: Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained tissue sections from various areas of the body should show nuclei with various chromatin patterns along with a crisp nuclear membrane. A properly stained section should show three shades of eosin staining. However, in certain instances sections stained with H&E are characterised by varied staining abnormalities. As a medical laboratory scientist, identify **six (6)** problems that could be encountered while staining tissues with H&E and propose **three (3)** ways to correct each problem. *(10 marks)*
answer:
| Problem | Causes / corrections |
|---|---|
| **Pale (weak) nuclear staining** | Stain longer in haematoxylin; replace exhausted or over-oxidised haematoxylin; reduce differentiation in acid alcohol; avoid prolonged decalcification/acid fixation |
| **Over-stained, dark nuclei with no chromatin detail** | Shorten haematoxylin time; differentiate adequately in acid alcohol; cut thinner sections |
| **Red/brown nuclei** (poor bluing) | Blue adequately in Scott's tap water substitute or running tap water; check pH of bluing agent; use fresh haematoxylin |
| **Pale eosin / no shades of eosin** | Use fresh eosin and correct pH (~4.5–5, add acetic acid); do not over-wash in water or low alcohols; stain longer |
| **Over-stained eosin (all one dark pink)** | Shorten eosin time; differentiate in 70–95% alcohol/water; dilute eosin |
| **Uneven/patchy staining** | Dewax completely (fresh xylene); hydrate fully before aqueous stains; keep sections from drying during staining |
| **Hazy, milky slides or water droplets under the coverslip** | Dehydrate fully in fresh absolute alcohol; change contaminated xylene; mount quickly |
| **Precipitate/deposit on section** | Filter haematoxylin daily; remove the metallic sheen; clean staining dishes |

> [!answer]
> Any six H&E faults (pale/dark nuclei, red nuclei, weak/strong eosin, patchy staining, hazy slides, precipitate) each with three corrections relating to time, reagent freshness/pH, differentiation, bluing, dewaxing and dehydration.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

H&E quality depends on **reagent quality** (ripening of haematoxylin, eosin pH), **timing** of each step, adequate **differentiation and bluing**, complete **dewaxing** and **dehydration/clearing**. A quality-control slide each day helps detect drifts.

## Simplified explanation

Most H&E problems come from wrong times, old or wrong-pH stains, poor bluing or differentiation, wax left behind or water left in the slide.
hint: Think about each step: dewaxing, haematoxylin, differentiation, bluing, eosin, dehydration, clearing.

body:
An organised aggregate of cells could function in a collective manner. This could be classified as...

(I) epithelial cell (II) connective tissue (III) muscle cells (IV) tissue

options.hint: An epithelial cell is a single cell, not an aggregate.
Correct. Connective tissue and 'tissue' are both organised aggregates of cells.
I and III are single cell types.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **tissue** is an organised aggregate of cells (with their extracellular matrix) functioning together. 'Connective tissue' and 'tissue' fit this definition; 'epithelial cell' and 'muscle cells' name cells, not tissues.

## Simplified explanation

Only the **tissues** (connective tissue, tissue) are groups working together.

body: A patient had acute inflammation of the colon for some months, with recent involvement of the anal canal. Under the light microscope, the anal canal is lined with stratified squamous epithelium. There are polymorph leukocytes within the epithelium, most often close to the surface. What economical staining technique can be employed to achieve this microscopic description?

options.hint: Correct. Routine, cheap and shows epithelium and inflammatory cells well.
A special stain for basement membranes/fungi.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**H&E** is the routine, economical stain: it shows epithelial architecture and inflammatory cells (neutrophil polymorphs with lobed nuclei) clearly. Special stains are reserved for specific substances.

## Simplified explanation

Use the routine, cheap **H&E**.

body: Under the light microscope, an ovoid abscess within the upper epidermis causing the surface to bulge upwards was apparent. Also seen was a thick layer of keratin on the surface of the skin. At a higher magnification, necrotic epithelial cells were also found to be present. What staining technique is just suitable for this demonstration?

options.hint: Correct. H&E shows the abscess, keratin and necrotic cells.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Abscesses, hyperkeratosis and necrosis are all **morphological** features well seen with routine **H&E** (keratin is pink, necrotic cells show pyknosis/karyorrhexis and eosinophilic cytoplasm).

## Simplified explanation

General tissue changes are seen with **H&E**.

body:
**Case:** Easy bruising, thin skin with visible veins, characteristic facial features, and rupture of arteries, uterus or intestines were among the common findings recorded by a family physician. To rule out Ehlers-Danlos type IV, a liver biopsy was taken and sent to the histopathology laboratory for light microscopic evaluation.

What suitable staining technique can be used to rule out, or otherwise, Ehlers-Danlos type IV?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type IV (vascular)** results from defective **type III collagen** (COL3A1). A **collagen stain** such as **Masson's trichrome** (collagen blue/green) is used to assess collagen at light-microscope level; confirmation is by genetic or biochemical testing.

## Simplified explanation

EDS affects collagen, so use a collagen stain: **Masson trichrome**.

body: **Case (continued):** Based on the selected staining technique for Ehlers-Danlos type IV (Masson trichrome), what will be the MOST suitable fixative for the preservation of the specimen prior to processing?

options.hint: Acceptable, but sections then need mordanting in Bouin's for best trichrome results.
Used within Bouin's but not alone.
Correct. Bouin's fluid gives the brightest trichrome staining.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Trichrome stains work best on tissue fixed in **Bouin's fluid** (picric acid, formalin, acetic acid), which enhances acid dye binding. Formalin-fixed sections are usually post-mordanted in Bouin's at 56 °C before Masson's trichrome.

## Simplified explanation

For trichrome, fix in **Bouin's**.

body: Collagen may be demonstrated more selectively by compound solutions of acid dyes. How are **different types** of collagen demonstrated? Through the application of...

options.hint: Correct. Type-specific antibodies distinguish collagen types I, II, III, IV etc.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Dye methods (van Gieson, trichromes) stain collagen in general. To distinguish **collagen types (I, III, IV…)**, **immunohistochemistry** with type-specific antibodies is used.

## Simplified explanation

To tell **types** of collagen apart, use **antibodies (IHC)**.

body: The predominant cell type in a connective tissue is...

options.hint: Correct. Fibroblasts are the principal and most numerous cells.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Fibroblasts** are the principal and most common cells of connective tissue; they synthesise collagen, elastic fibres and ground substance.

## Simplified explanation

**Fibroblasts** are the main connective tissue cells.

body: Which of the following connective tissue cell types has a flattened nucleus at the periphery?

options.hint: Macrophages have an indented, oval nucleus.
Correct. A large fat droplet pushes the nucleus to the edge (signet-ring).

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In **unilocular (white) adipocytes** a single large lipid droplet fills the cell, compressing the nucleus into a **flattened crescent at the periphery** (signet-ring appearance).

## Simplified explanation

Fat cells push their nucleus flat to the side: **adipocytes**.

body: Which of the following stains can be used to selectively demonstrate collagen?

options.hint: Correct. MSB stains collagen blue, fibrin red, red cells yellow.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Martius scarlet blue** is a trichrome: **collagen blue**, fibrin red, erythrocytes yellow, nuclei blue-black. Other collagen stains: van Gieson, Masson's trichrome. Sudan black B and Oil red O are lipid stains.

## Simplified explanation

**MSB** stains collagen blue.

body: The epithelium that lines the walls and covers the contents of the closed cavities of the body, such as pericardial and pleural, is termed...

options.hint: Correct. Lines serous cavities (pleura, pericardium, peritoneum).

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Mesothelium** is the simple squamous epithelium lining the serous cavities (pleural, pericardial, peritoneal) and covering the organs within them. Endothelium lines vessels; endocardium lines the heart.

## Simplified explanation

Body cavities are lined by **mesothelium**.

body: Based on shape and the number of layers, epithelial tissues are subclassified into simple columnar, simple squamous, stratified squamous, etc. A specimen from the **bladder** was received at the pathology department; it was processed and stained with H&E. The specimen shows NORMAL morphology. Name and describe the type of epithelial tissue likely to be viewed. *(7 marks)*
answer:
**Transitional epithelium (urothelium).**

- A **stratified** epithelium, about 3–7 cell layers thick in the relaxed (empty) bladder.
- **Basal cells** are small and cuboidal/columnar; intermediate cells are polygonal.
- **Surface (umbrella) cells** are large, **dome-shaped**, sometimes binucleate, with a thickened apical plasma membrane (plaques) forming a permeability barrier.
- When the bladder is **distended**, the epithelium thins to 2–3 layers and the surface cells **flatten** (resembling stratified squamous).
- Rests on a basement membrane over lamina propria and the detrusor muscle.

> [!answer]
> Transitional epithelium (urothelium): stratified, with dome-shaped umbrella surface cells that flatten when the bladder is stretched.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Urothelium is specialised to **stretch** and to be **impermeable to urine**. Its umbrella cells have uroplakin plaques and folded membranes that unfold during distension, so the number of apparent layers and the shape of surface cells change with bladder filling.

## Simplified explanation

The bladder is lined by **transitional epithelium**: several layers with dome-shaped top cells that flatten when the bladder fills.

body: What should be the minimum volume of fixative to tissue?

options.text: At least 2 times the volume of tissue
At most 5 times the volume of tissue
At least 10 times the volume of tissue
At most 10 times the volume of tissue
options.hint: It is a minimum, not a maximum.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Fixative volume should be **at least 10 times** (ideally 15–20 times) the tissue volume so the fixative is not depleted and fixation is uniform.

## Simplified explanation

Use **at least 10 times** more fixative than tissue.

body: You received a tissue biopsy at the reception and upon inspection, you noticed the container is **leaky**. What is the most appropriate thing to do?

options.hint: Correct. A leaking container is a biohazard and a recognised rejection criterion.

options.text: Fill the container with appropriate fixative and proceed

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Leaking containers are a **biosafety hazard** and may mean loss of fixative or specimen and contamination of the request form. Laboratory **rejection criteria** include leaking containers, unlabelled/mislabelled specimens and missing request forms; the clinician is informed so it can be corrected.

## Simplified explanation

A **leaking container** is rejected (and the ward informed).

body: An autopsy specimen received at the reception was not accompanied by a request form. What is the most appropriate thing to do?

options.text: Receive the specimen and fill one of the requisition forms
options.hint: Laboratory staff must not fill in clinical requests.
Correct. A specimen without a request form should not be accepted.

options.text: Collect the specimen and discard it
Process such specimen but remember to document your observation

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The request form carries patient identification, clinical details and the investigation required. A specimen **without a request form** is **rejected** (the requesting clinician is notified) – laboratory staff should never complete the request themselves.

## Simplified explanation

No request form → **reject** and inform the sender.

body: A biopsy was received at the reception and the receptionist noticed that the volume of fixative is the same as that of the tissue. Advise the receptionist.

options.text: Such specimen ought to be rejected
options.hint: Rejection is unnecessary; the problem can be corrected.
The tissue will be poorly fixed.

options.text: Discard the old fixative and apply the appropriate volume of the same preservative
options.hint: Correct. Top up/replace with the correct volume (10–20×) of the same fixative.

options.text: Discard the old fixative and apply the appropriate volume of a different preservative
options.hint: Changing fixative type could interfere with later tests.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A 1:1 tissue-to-fixative ratio leads to **inadequate fixation**. Correct it by replacing/topping up with an **adequate volume (≥10–20×) of the same fixative**, so fixation continues uniformly with the same chemistry.

## Simplified explanation

Add enough of the **same** fixative.

body: Which of the following is a **non-coagulant** fixative?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Non-coagulant fixatives**: formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde, **osmium tetroxide**, potassium dichromate, acetic acid. **Coagulant**: alcohols, acetone, picric acid, mercuric chloride, chromic acid, TCA.

## Simplified explanation

**Osmium tetroxide** does not coagulate proteins.

body: Which of the following is a **coagulant** fixative?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Mercuric chloride** reacts with proteins (especially sulphydryl groups) and **coagulates** them; it gives excellent nuclear detail (Zenker's, Helly's, B5) but leaves mercury pigment.

## Simplified explanation

**Mercuric chloride** is a coagulant fixative.

body: Which of the following is **not** considered an aqueous fixative?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Acetone** is used neat and cold as a non-aqueous, coagulant fixative (e.g. for enzymes and frozen sections). Formaldehyde, glyoxal and picric acid are used as **aqueous** solutions.

## Simplified explanation

**Acetone** is not water-based.

body: The issue where small pieces of tissue fragments are carried from one tissue to the next is termed...

options.hint: Correct. Carryover (floaters) from one specimen to another.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Tissue carryover (contamination, 'floaters')** occurs when fragments from one specimen are transferred to another – at grossing (dirty instruments/board), processing or on the water bath. It can cause misdiagnosis, so instruments and baths are cleaned between cases.

## Simplified explanation

Bits of one tissue ending up with another = **carryover**.

body: Which of the following is **not** a suitable clearing agent?

options.hint: Correct. Benzene is carcinogenic, so it is unsuitable for routine use.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Benzene** clears rapidly but is a **known human carcinogen** (leukaemia), so it is no longer considered suitable. Xylene, toluene, chloroform and xylene substitutes are used instead.

## Simplified explanation

**Benzene** causes cancer, so it is not suitable.

body: Which of the following is **not** associated with incomplete dehydration of tissue?

options.text: Clearing agents will not act properly
options.hint: Residual water makes clearant turn milky.
Water left in tissue keeps it soft.
Correct. Hard, brittle tissue results from over-dehydration, not incomplete dehydration.
Poor infiltration gives a mushy block.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Incomplete dehydration leaves water, so the **clearing agent turns milky**, wax cannot infiltrate, and the tissue is **soft and mushy** and crumbles. **Hardness/brittleness** results from **prolonged** dehydration or overheating.

## Simplified explanation

Not enough dehydration → soft and mushy, not **hard**.

body: Which of the following is **not** an infiltration agent?

options.hint: Correct. Chloroform is a clearing agent.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Infiltration/embedding media include **paraffin wax**, **celloidin (nitrocellulose)**, gelatin, carbowax and **resins** (epoxy, acrylic). **Chloroform** is a clearing agent.

## Simplified explanation

**Chloroform** clears; it does not infiltrate.

body: The process of enclosing the tissue in an infiltration medium and allowing it to solidify is termed...

options.hint: Infiltration fills the tissue with medium.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Embedding (blocking)** encloses the infiltrated tissue in fresh medium in a mould, correctly oriented, and lets it solidify into a block.

## Simplified explanation

Setting tissue in a wax block = **blocking (embedding)**.

body: What term is applicable when the dye and the substance to be dyed develop different charges and thus become attracted to each other?

options.hint: Correct. Attraction of opposite charges (salt linkage).
Weak bonds between H and electronegative atoms.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Electrostatic (ionic, salt) bonding** is the main mechanism of most dyeing: anionic (acid) dyes bind cationic tissue groups (–NH₃⁺) and cationic (basic) dyes bind anionic groups (phosphate, sulphate, carboxyl).

## Simplified explanation

Opposite charges attract: **electrostatic bonding**.

body: Formalin has the potential of...

options.hint: Correct. Formalin blocks amino groups, so fewer cationic sites bind acid dyes.
Formalin does not block the anionic groups responsible for basophilia.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Formaldehyde reacts with **amino (–NH₂) groups**, which are the cationic sites that bind **acid dyes (eosin)**. Blocking them **reduces acidophilia** (eosinophilia); basophilia (phosphate groups of nucleic acids) is little affected.

## Simplified explanation

Formalin blocks the groups eosin sticks to, so it **reduces acidophilia**.

body: Tissue retention of dyes or stains is dependent on ...

options.hint: The medium is removed before staining.
Correct. The fixative alters reactive groups and hence dye binding and retention.
Affects intensity, but retention depends on how dye binds the fixed tissue.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The **fixative** changes the number and nature of reactive groups (e.g. formalin blocks amino groups, mercury enhances acid dye binding, Bouin's promotes trichrome staining), so how well a tissue **takes up and retains dyes** depends largely on fixation.

## Simplified explanation

How dyes stay in tissue depends on the **fixative used**.

body: Increasing the temperature of a dye can lead to...

options.hint: Temperature does not set the dye charge (pH does).

options.text: Increase rate of diffusion of the dye
options.hint: Correct. Heat speeds diffusion/penetration of dye into tissue.
Faster staining, but the defining effect is faster diffusion; over-staining is controlled by time.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Raising temperature **increases the rate of diffusion** (and reaction) of dye into tissue, shortening staining times (e.g. heated Ziehl–Neelsen carbol fuchsin, microwave staining). It also swells tissue, helping penetration.

## Simplified explanation

Heat makes the dye **move in faster**.

body: Haematein is...

options.hint: It becomes cationic only with a mordant.
Correct. Haematein alone is a weakly anionic dye with poor affinity for tissue.
The haematein–metal lake is cationic, not haematein itself.

hint: It needs a mordant to stain nuclei.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Haematein** (oxidised haematoxylin) is **weakly anionic** and has little affinity for tissue. Combined with a **mordant** (aluminium, iron) it forms a **cationic dye–metal lake** that binds the phosphate groups of nuclear DNA.

## Simplified explanation

Haematein alone is **weakly anionic**; the mordant makes it a nuclear stain.

body: Natural ripening of haematoxylin (to haematein) can be achieved by one of these...

options.hint: Correct. Exposure to air and sunlight is natural ripening.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Natural ripening** = slow oxidation by **air and sunlight** over weeks–months (e.g. Ehrlich's, Delafield's). **Chemical ripening** uses oxidants such as **sodium iodate** (Mayer's) or **mercuric oxide** (Harris').

## Simplified explanation

Natural ripening uses **sunlight and air**.

body: Haematoxylin (haematein) is a ...

options.hint: The lake behaves basically, but the expected answer is its use as a nuclear stain.
Correct. Haematoxylin is the standard nuclear stain.

hint: In H&E, which part does it stain?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

With a mordant, haematoxylin stains **nuclei** blue (chromatin), so it is classed as a **nuclear dye**; eosin is the cytoplasmic counterstain.

## Simplified explanation

Haematoxylin colours the **nucleus**.

body: Eosin is a ...

options.hint: Correct. Eosin is an acid dye staining cytoplasm and fibres pink.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Eosin Y** is an anionic (acid) xanthene dye that stains **cytoplasm**, collagen, muscle and red cells in shades of pink/red.

## Simplified explanation

Eosin stains the **cytoplasm** pink.

body: Abnormal deposition of misfolded proteins leading to aggregation to form insoluble fibrils in the extracellular compartment is termed what?

options.hint: Correct. Extracellular insoluble fibrillar protein with β-pleated sheet structure.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Amyloid** is extracellular, insoluble fibrillar protein formed from misfolded precursor proteins (AL light chains, serum amyloid A, transthyretin, β2-microglobulin, Aβ…) that adopt a **cross-β-pleated sheet** conformation, giving Congo red apple-green birefringence.

## Simplified explanation

Misfolded proteins clumped outside cells = **amyloid**.

body: One of these is **not** likely to be associated with amyloidosis

options.text: Shortness of breath with minimal exertion
Swelling of your ankles and legs

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Systemic amyloidosis typically causes **fatigue and weakness**, **breathlessness** (cardiac amyloid), **oedema of ankles/legs** (nephrotic syndrome or heart failure), weight loss, macroglossia, neuropathy and foamy (proteinuric) urine. Frequent urination is not a characteristic feature.

## Simplified explanation

Tiredness, breathlessness and leg swelling are typical; **frequent urination** is not.

body: In the demonstration of amyloid in tissue using the Congo red method, what is the preferred thickness of the section?

options.hint: Too thin: weak staining and birefringence.
Correct. Thicker sections (8–10 µm) show apple-green birefringence clearly.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Congo red staining and its **apple-green birefringence** under polarised light are more easily seen in **thicker sections (8–10 µm)** than in routine 3–5 µm sections, avoiding false negatives with small deposits.

## Simplified explanation

Cut Congo red sections **8–10 µm** thick.

body: When the H & E staining technique is adopted, what will be the result (colour) for amyloid?

options.hint: Green is the birefringence colour with Congo red.
Correct. Amyloid is pale pink, amorphous and eosinophilic in H&E.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In **H&E**, amyloid appears as **pale pink**, amorphous, glassy (hyaline) extracellular material. Special stains (Congo red, Sirius red, thioflavin T) confirm it.

## Simplified explanation

With H&E amyloid looks **pale pink**.

body: When the Congo red staining technique is adopted, how will amyloid appear (under ordinary light)?

options.hint: Apple-green is seen only under polarised light.
Correct. Amyloid stains red (orange-red) with Congo red.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

With **Congo red**, amyloid stains **red/orange-red** in bright-field and shows **apple-green birefringence** under polarised light (the confirmatory feature).

## Simplified explanation

Congo red makes amyloid **red** (green only under polarised light).

body: When the Sirius red staining technique is adopted, what will be the result (colour) of the amyloid?

options.hint: Correct. Sirius red stains amyloid red.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Alkaline **Sirius red** (Llewellyn) stains amyloid **red**, with birefringence under polarised light, similar to Congo red.

## Simplified explanation

Sirius red stains amyloid **red**.

body: When the Thioflavin staining technique is adopted, what will be the result (colour) of the amyloid?

options.hint: Correct. Thioflavin T gives yellow-green fluorescence under UV/blue light.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Thioflavin T** binds amyloid and gives bright **yellow-green fluorescence** under UV/blue excitation; it is sensitive but less specific than Congo red.

## Simplified explanation

Thioflavin makes amyloid glow **green**.

body: A coloured agent deposited frequently as cytoplasmic inclusions or granules in cells and tissues may be termed

options.hint: Correct. Pigments are coloured substances in cells and tissues.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Pigments** are substances with their own **colour**, found in cells and tissues as granules or deposits. They are **endogenous** (haematogenous: haemosiderin, bilirubin; non-haematogenous: melanin, lipofuscin), **exogenous** (carbon, tattoo) or **artefact** (formalin, mercury pigment).

## Simplified explanation

Coloured granules in tissue are **pigments**.

body: A black pigment commonly seen in sections from the lung and associated lymph nodes is called...

options.hint: Correct. Inhaled carbon (anthracotic pigment) is black.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Carbon (anthracotic pigment)** is an exogenous pigment inhaled from smoke and polluted air; it is phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages and carried to hilar lymph nodes. It is black and resists bleaching and solvents.

## Simplified explanation

Black pigment in lungs = **carbon**.

body: Which of the following is likely to be found in the lungs of a person who has been exposed to large quantities of asbestos?

options.hint: Bare fibres are present but the characteristic finding is coated fibres.
Correct. Ferruginous (asbestos) bodies: fibres coated with iron-protein.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Inhaled asbestos fibres become coated with **iron-containing protein (haemosiderin)**, forming golden-brown, beaded, dumbbell-shaped **asbestos (ferruginous) bodies**, which stain with Perls' Prussian blue.

## Simplified explanation

Asbestos exposure gives **asbestos bodies** in the lung.

body: Haemosiderin is considered as...

options.hint: Correct. Derived from haemoglobin breakdown in the body.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Haemosiderin** is an **endogenous haematogenous** pigment: an iron-storage complex derived from haemoglobin breakdown, seen as golden-brown granules and stained blue by Perls' Prussian blue.

## Simplified explanation

Haemosiderin is made in the body: **endogenous**.

body: Which of the following is classified as an endogenous **non-haematogenous** pigment?

options.hint: Correct. Lipofuscin derives from lipid peroxidation, not blood.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Endogenous haematogenous** pigments come from haemoglobin (haemosiderin, bilirubin/bile, haematoidin, porphyrins). **Endogenous non-haematogenous** pigments include **lipofuscin**, ceroid and **melanin**.

## Simplified explanation

**Lipofuscin** is not derived from blood.

body: Which type of pigment is ceroid?

options.hint: Correct. Ceroid is a lipopigment like lipofuscin.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Ceroid** is a **lipopigment** (oxidised lipid-protein complex) closely related to lipofuscin, so it is an **endogenous non-haematogenous** pigment; it is acid-fast and Sudan black positive.

## Simplified explanation

Ceroid is a fat-derived pigment made in the body: **endogenous non-haematogenous**.

body: Which of the following stain techniques is most suitable for the demonstration of ferric iron (Fe³⁺)?

options.hint: Correct. Perls' Prussian blue demonstrates ferric iron.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Perls' Prussian blue**: acid releases ferric ions, which react with potassium ferrocyanide to form insoluble blue **ferric ferrocyanide**. It demonstrates haemosiderin/ferric iron.

## Simplified explanation

Ferric iron → **Prussian blue**.

body: When idiopathic haemochromatosis is suspected, which of the following demonstrations can be considered useful?

options.hint: Correct. Haemochromatosis is iron overload (haemosiderin in liver, pancreas, heart).

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Hereditary (idiopathic) haemochromatosis** causes excessive iron absorption with **haemosiderin (ferric iron) deposits** in hepatocytes, pancreas and heart, demonstrated by **Perls' Prussian blue** on liver biopsy.

## Simplified explanation

Haemochromatosis = too much iron, so stain for **ferric iron**.

body: Turnbull blue stain is used for the demonstration of...

options.hint: Shown with Perls' (they contain ferric iron).
Correct. Turnbull blue uses potassium ferricyanide to detect ferrous iron.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Turnbull's blue** reaction uses **potassium ferricyanide** in acid, which reacts with **ferrous (Fe²⁺) iron** to give a blue precipitate. Ferrous iron is rare in tissue, so ferric iron may first be reduced (ammonium sulphide) to apply the method.

## Simplified explanation

Turnbull blue → **ferrous iron**.

body: The von Kossa staining technique can be used to demonstrate...

options.hint: Correct. Silver replaces calcium in calcium salts (phosphate/carbonate), reduced to black silver.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In **von Kossa's method**, silver ions replace calcium bound to phosphate/carbonate; light reduces the silver salt to **black metallic silver**. It indirectly demonstrates **calcium** deposits. Alizarin red S binds calcium directly (orange-red).

## Simplified explanation

Von Kossa shows **calcium** as black.

body: Which of the following can serve as a suitable positive control for the demonstration of calcium using the Alizarin red S staining method?

options.hint: Correct. A positive control must contain the substance.

hint: A positive control must contain the target.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **positive control** is a section **known to contain the substance** being demonstrated (e.g. calcified tissue, bone, a calcified lesion); it confirms the reagents and technique are working.

## Simplified explanation

Use a section that you **know contains calcium**.

body: Which of the following staining techniques can be used to demonstrate lipids?

options.hint: Correct. A lysochrome (fat-soluble dye) for neutral lipids.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Oil red O** (and Sudan III, Sudan IV, Sudan black B) are **lysochromes**: dyes more soluble in lipid than in their solvent, so they move into fat droplets, staining them red.

## Simplified explanation

**Oil red O** stains fat.

body: To demonstrate neutral fat using the Oil red O method, what is the most suitable fixative?

options.hint: Correct. Formalin (NBF/formal calcium) preserves lipids for frozen sections.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Lipids are dissolved by alcohols and clearing agents, so lipid stains use **formalin-fixed (10% NBF or formal calcium) frozen sections** that are not processed through solvents.

## Simplified explanation

Fix in **10% NBF** (alcohol would dissolve the fat).

body: In the demonstration of neutral fat using Oil red O, which of the following can serve as the MOST suitable positive control?

options.hint: Fatty liver can be used, but not the expected answer here.

options.text: Positive control may not be necessary
options.hint: Correct. Adipose tissue present in most sections acts as an internal control.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Most tissue sections contain some **adipose tissue** that stains with Oil red O, acting as a built-in **internal positive control**, so a separate positive control is often regarded as unnecessary (a known fatty tissue can still be used for QC).

## Simplified explanation

Fat cells already in the section show the stain worked.

body: In the demonstration of neutral fat using Oil red O, what should be the thickness of the section?
hint: Lipids are lost in paraffin processing.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Neutral fat is dissolved by the alcohols and xylene of paraffin processing, so lipid stains are done on **frozen sections**, typically **8–10 µm** thick.

## Simplified explanation

Use **frozen sections 8–10 µm** thick.

body: What is the expected result (colour of fat) when the Oil red O staining method is used?
hint: The dye's name gives it away.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Oil red O**: neutral lipids **red**, nuclei blue (haematoxylin counterstain).

## Simplified explanation

Fat goes **red**.

body: Sudan black B is a suitable technique for the demonstration of ...

options.hint: Correct. Sudan black B is a lysochrome for lipids (including phospholipids).

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Sudan black B** is a lysochrome that stains neutral lipids and phospholipids **blue-black**; it also stains lipofuscin and granulocyte granules.

## Simplified explanation

Sudan black B stains **lipids**.

body: In immunohistochemistry, how are masked epitopes (antigens) retrieved?

options.text: Inducing epitope with heat or enzyme
options.hint: Correct. Heat-induced (HIER) or proteolytic enzyme-induced (PIER) epitope retrieval.

options.text: Through processing of tissue in xylene

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Formalin crosslinks **mask epitopes**. **Antigen retrieval** reverses this by **heat-induced epitope retrieval** (microwave, pressure cooker or water bath in citrate/EDTA buffer) or **proteolytic enzyme digestion** (trypsin, proteinase K, pepsin).

## Simplified explanation

Heat or enzymes **unmask** the antigens.

body: In immunohistochemistry, how do you overcome endogenous proteins that have the potential of interfering with the outcome?

options.hint: Correct. Blocking steps (serum/protein block, peroxidase block, avidin–biotin block).

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Blocking** prevents non-specific staining: normal serum/BSA blocks hydrophobic and Fc binding; **H₂O₂/methanol** blocks endogenous peroxidase; avidin–biotin blocking for endogenous biotin; levamisole for alkaline phosphatase.

## Simplified explanation

Use a **blocking** step.

body: One of the following is a MAJOR requirement during immunohistochemistry analysis

options.hint: The target, not a requirement of the run.
Also needed, but the expected answer is the positive control.
Correct. A known positive tissue validates every run.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Every IHC run needs a **positive control** (tissue known to express the antigen) to show the antibody, retrieval and detection worked; negative controls (omitting primary antibody) detect non-specific staining. Without a working positive control, a negative result cannot be interpreted.

## Simplified explanation

You must show the stain works on a **positive control**.
